Connect the finding to the decision.

Observed
Some children could not spell their names or recall their student IDs. The director was already signing students in individually.
Constraint
Student information could not be openly exposed, and school network/API access was not available to the team.
Team decision
Move attendance to a separate director screen with bulk sign-in.
Feedback
Staff responded positively. The documented outcome is qualitative; no measured time savings are claimed.

A request like “review this project” leaves the person delegating it with unanswered questions: what can the assistant access, which steps will it take, and when will it stop?

I designed the review around those decisions. Users inspect a draft before a run, approve consequential actions individually, and check an interrupted action’s result before retrying.

This is an independent project based on my browser-assistant research and specifications. The application screens below show an installation preview, not a connected runtime.

The question

What can the assistant access, which steps will it take, and when will it stop?

My design response

Make the workflow reviewable before execution, with approval tied to the specific action and draft.

Independent browser-assistant research and specifications. Screens show an installation preview, not a connected runtime.
The original pseudocode tracked completion but left cancellation, recovery and replay unresolved.
The original plan tracked completion, but did not settle what happens when work is canceled, interrupted or tried again.
Show uncertain outcomes, block interrupted writes from replaying, and ask for evidence before continuing.
Show when the result is uncertain. Check whether a change happened before sending the same action again.
Repairs addressed cancellation races, stale approvals and possible duplicate dispatch.
Fixes addressed competing cancellation events, approval of outdated drafts and the risk of sending an action twice.
This is intended to prevent the same write from being sent twice.
This is intended to prevent the same change from being sent twice.

Approve the specific action.

Browser origins, workspace access and native runtime connection are separate concerns. Consequential steps require one-time approval tied to the workflow revision and action.

Separate the access decisions.

Browser origins, workspace access and native runtime connection each have a separate access boundary. The approval model above governs the action that follows.

Check interrupted actions before retrying.

The app saves a recovery checkpoint before sending an action. If an interruption leaves the outcome unclear, it blocks another attempt until the result is checked.

Save the recovery checkpoint first.

The app stores recovery state before sending an action. That checkpoint supports the result check described in the research story.
Taska ties each consequential approval to a specific step and workflow revision.
Taska ties each one-time approval to a specific step and workflow revision.
